title: The Richest Man in Babylon
author: George S. Clason
pd: published 1926; public domain in India and the United States
text:
The Richest Man in Babylon, by George S. Clason. The whole book, chapter by chapter. This is a book that dresses up some of the most important financial wisdom ever distilled in the robes of ancient Babylon, using parables and stories set five thousand years ago to teach lessons that remain just as relevant today. Clason wrote these stories in the 1920s, originally as a series of pamphlets distributed by banks and insurance companies, and they became so popular that they were collected into a book that has never gone out of print. The genius of the book is its simplicity. There are no complex formulas here, no sophisticated investment strategies, no jargon. Just clear, timeless principles about how to build wealth, told through the voices of characters you come to care about.

The book opens with the story of Bansir, a chariot builder, and Kobbi, a musician, two men who have worked hard their entire lives but have nothing to show for it. They are skilled at their trades but perpetually broke, living from one payment to the next, watching the wealthy merchants and traders of Babylon enjoy lives of comfort and abundance while they struggle. They decide to seek out their childhood friend Arkad, who has become the richest man in the city, and ask him how he did it. Arkad's answer is the foundation of the entire book: he didn't earn more than anyone else. He simply learned the laws of gold and followed them with discipline.

The first and most famous principle is to pay yourself first. Arkad learned this from a money lender named Algamish, who told him that a part of all you earn is yours to keep. Not what's left over after expenses. Not what you manage to save if there's anything remaining at the end of the month. At least one-tenth of everything you earn should be set aside before you pay anyone else, before you buy food, before you pay rent, before you indulge in any pleasure. This sounds almost too simple to be useful, but Clason's point is that most people never do it. They assume they will save whatever is left over, and there is never anything left over because expenses expand to fill whatever income is available. The only way to break this cycle is to treat savings as a non-negotiable obligation to yourself, as sacred as any debt you owe to others.

The second principle is to control your expenditures. Clason makes the observation that what we call necessary expenses will always grow to equal our incomes unless we protest to the contrary. A person earning twice as much as their neighbor doesn't automatically have twice as much left over. They simply find twice as many things to spend money on. The cure is to examine every expense and ask whether it is truly necessary or merely a desire masquerading as a need. Clason doesn't advocate for a life of deprivation. He advocates for conscious spending, knowing where your money goes and making deliberate choices about what deserves your hard-earned gold.

The third principle is to make your gold multiply. Saving money is essential, but it's only the first step. The real power comes from putting your savings to work, investing them in ventures that generate returns, which in turn generate their own returns. Clason describes this as your gold working for you, laboring day and night to produce more gold, which then produces more gold still. This is the ancient version of compound interest, and Clason understood its power as well as any modern financial advisor. The money you save and invest today doesn't just grow by the amount you add to it. It grows by its own earnings, and those earnings grow by their earnings, and over time this process produces results that seem almost magical.

The fourth principle is to guard your treasure from loss. Clason tells stories of people who lost their savings by investing in ventures they didn't understand, trusting smooth-talking strangers with their money, or chasing unrealistic returns. Arkad himself made this mistake early in his journey, entrusting his first year's savings to a brickmaker who had a friend with a scheme to buy jewels from distant lands. The brickmaker knew nothing about jewels, the friend was a fraud, and the money was lost. The lesson is stark: the first sound principle of investment is security of the principal. Before you worry about returns, make sure you won't lose what you've already saved. Invest only with people who know what they're doing, in ventures you understand, and never risk money you cannot afford to lose.

The fifth principle is to make your dwelling a profitable investment. Clason argues that owning your own home is one of the wisest financial decisions a person can make, because the money you would otherwise spend on rent goes instead toward building equity in something you own. The payments feel burdensome at first, but they end, whereas rent never does. And the sense of pride and stability that comes from owning your own home has benefits that go beyond the financial.

The sixth principle is to ensure a future income. Clason understood that youth and health are temporary, and that a wise person prepares for the time when they can no longer work. This means setting aside money specifically for retirement, for the care of your family after you're gone, and for the inevitable periods of illness or misfortune that every life contains. This isn't pessimism. It's prudence. The person who plans for the future doesn't live in fear of it. They live with the confidence that comes from knowing they are prepared.

The seventh principle is to increase your ability to earn. Clason argues that your most valuable asset is your ability to produce income, and that investing in yourself, your skills, your knowledge, your capacity to do useful work, is the highest-return investment you can make. The person who becomes more skilled commands higher compensation. The person who understands their craft deeply finds opportunities invisible to others. Study your trade, seek mentors, read widely, practice diligently, and your earning power will grow in ways that amplify all the other principles.

Beyond these core principles, the book contains several memorable stories that reinforce and expand upon them. There is the story of Dabasir, a former slave who clawed his way back to prosperity through disciplined adherence to these principles, repaying every debt and rebuilding his life one careful step at a time. There is the story of Sharru Nada, who teaches a young man the value of hard work by sharing his own journey from slave to wealthy merchant. There is the story of the walls of Babylon, which serves as a metaphor for the importance of protecting what you have built, whether through insurance, diversification, or simply the discipline to say no to risky propositions.

What makes this book endure is not the sophistication of its advice but its profound simplicity. These principles are not secrets. They are not hidden knowledge available only to the wealthy or the educated. They are available to anyone who has the discipline to follow them. And that is Clason's deepest insight: the obstacle to financial security is not lack of knowledge but lack of discipline. We all know we should save, invest wisely, avoid debt, and live within our means. The question is whether we actually do it. The stories in this book, simple as they are, have a way of making these principles vivid and memorable, giving them an emotional weight that dry financial advice never achieves.

The bottom line: The Richest Man in Babylon teaches that wealth is built not through high income or clever tricks but through a handful of timeless principles: save a fixed portion of everything you earn, invest it wisely, protect it from loss, and continuously increase your ability to earn. Discipline, not intelligence, is the key to financial security.
